name: King Crimson
description:
'''King Crimson''' were an English [[progressive rock]] band formed in London in 1968. Led by guitarist and primary composer [[Robert Fripp]]{{Spaced en dash}}the group's sole constant member throughout their history{{Spaced en dash}}the band are widely regarded as a foundational catalyst of the progressive rock movement. They drew inspiration from an expansive array of musical styles, incorporating elements of [[classical music|classical]], [[jazz]], [[folk music|folk]], [[heavy metal music|heavy metal]], [[gamelan]], [[post-punk]], [[Industrial music|industrial]], and [[experimental music]]. Beyond shaping contemporaries such as [[Yes (band)|Yes]] and [[Genesis (band)|Genesis]], King Crimson's genre-spanning innovations have exerted a lasting influence on subsequent generations of alternative rock, metal, and math rock artists, earning the band an enduring global [[cult following]].

The band was formed by Fripp, [[Michael Giles]], [[Greg Lake]], [[Ian McDonald (musician)|Ian McDonald]], and [[Peter Sinfield]]. Their debut album, ''[[In the Court of the Crimson King]]'' (1969), achieved immediate critical and commercial success, and is widely cited by music historians as a definitive cornerstone of progressive rock. Following the rapid dissolution of the original line-up, the group endured a period of personnel instability, during which time they released ''[[In the Wake of Poseidon]]'', ''[[Lizard (album)|Lizard]]'' (both 1970), and ''[[Islands (King Crimson album)|Islands]]'' (1971). In 1972, Fripp refashioned the band's direction by recruiting [[Bill Bruford]] (formerly of [[Yes (band)|Yes]]), [[John Wetton]], [[David Cross (musician)|David Cross]], and [[Jamie Muir]]. Leaning heavily into European [[free improvisation]] and avant-garde classical structures, the group produced three acclaimed studio albums during this period – ''[[Larks' Tongues in Aspic]]'' (1973), ''[[Starless and Bible Black]]'', and ''[[Red (King Crimson album)|Red]]'' (both 1974) – before Fripp disbanded the group at the end of 1974.

King Crimson returned from a seven-year hiatus in 1981 with a revamped, transatlantic line-up featuring Fripp, Bruford, and American musicians [[Adrian Belew]] and [[Tony Levin]]. Incorporating elements of New York [[Minimal music|minimalism]], gamelan, and contemporary [[new wave music|new wave]], this iteration recorded a distinct trilogy of studio albums: ''[[Discipline (King Crimson album)|Discipline]]'' (1981), ''[[Beat (King Crimson album)|Beat]]'' (1982), and ''[[Three of a Perfect Pair]]'' (1984). After another decade-long dormancy, the band reconstituted in 1994 as a "Double Trio" sextet, adding [[Pat Mastelotto]] and [[Trey Gunn]] to release ''[[Thrak]]'' (1995). During the late 1990s, the band members also operated in smaller, improvised sub-groups known as "[[ProjeKcts]]". The main group continued into the early 2000s as a "Double Duo" quartet, releasing ''[[The Construkction of Light|The ConstruKction of Light]]'' (2000) and ''[[The Power to Believe]]'' (2003), which showcased a heavier, industrial-influenced sound.

Following a brief 40th-anniversary tour in 2008 that introduced drummer [[Gavin Harrison]], Fripp placed the group on hold until 2013. King Crimson then re-emerged as a highly structured touring septet (and later octet) featuring an unusual three-drummer frontline and lead vocalist [[Jakko Jakszyk]]. This final incarnation spent seven years performing extensively rearranged material from across the band's entire [[King Crimson discography|historical discography]], backed by a massive archive of live releases. King Crimson permanently ceased activity at the conclusion of their December 2021 Japanese tour, with Fripp announcing that the band had officially "moved from sound to silence".
